stem: A nurse is caring for an adult client with a newly placed tracheostomy in an acute-care unit. Which emergency equipment should be kept immediately available at the bedside?

options.A: A replacement tracheostomy tube, an obturator, a bag-valve-mask device, and a suction catheter setup
options.B: A pulse oximeter, stethoscope, and oxygen tubing, with replacement airway equipment stored on the unit
options.C: A spare tracheostomy tube of the same size and tracheostomy ties, without a bag-valve-mask or suction setup
options.D: An oral airway and incentive spirometer, with tracheostomy replacement equipment brought only if decannulation occurs

rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills states that a replacement tracheostomy tube, an obturator, a bag-valve-mask device, and a suction catheter kit must be available in the room for patient safety. The same chapter also specifies bedside access to the obturator, spare tracheostomy tubes including the same size and one size smaller, and a bag-valve-mask device. Therefore A is the best answer. Monitoring equipment alone does not replace airway-rescue equipment; a same-size spare tube without ventilation and suction capability is incomplete; and oral-airway/incentive-spirometry equipment does not address an acute tracheostomy airway emergency.
educational_objective: Maintain immediate bedside access to essential tracheostomy emergency equipment, including a replacement tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask device, and suction setup, so airway patency and ventilation can be rapidly supported if the tracheostomy becomes obstructed or displaced.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine — NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Nursing Skills, 2nd edition — Chapter 22: Tracheostomy Care & Suctioning
source_version_date: 2nd edition, 2023; current NCBI Bookshelf page accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Chapter 22, section 22.2 Basic Concepts Related to Suctioning, bedside safety-equipment paragraph: obturator readily available; spare tracheostomy tubes same size and one size smaller; bag-valve-mask at bedside. Section 22.5 Checklist for Tracheostomy Suctioning, safety note: replacement tracheostomy tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask, and suction catheter kit must always be available in the room.
source_claim_supported: Acute-care tracheostomy patients require immediately available airway-rescue equipment including a replacement tracheostomy tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask device, and suction equipment; the chapter also specifies same-size and one-size-smaller spare tubes.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, p. 14: perform emergency care procedures; perform suctioning; provide care for clients with alterations in ventilation and oxygenation.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — tracheostomy airway emergency preparedness
correction_summary: Replaced the generic AARC homepage citation with an exact NCBI Nursing Skills locator that directly supports the bedside equipment claim. Rebuilt the keyed option to include the full core emergency set explicitly supported by the source, replaced obvious/filler distractors with clinically plausible but incomplete alternatives, and corrected the blueprint from Safety and Infection Prevention and Control to Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings: A directly matches the NCBI emergency-equipment statement. B provides monitoring but omits immediate rescue equipment; C is incomplete because ventilation and suction capability are absent; D does not provide tracheostomy-specific rescue equipment. No alternative is equally defensible. The stem specifies acute care and a new tracheostomy, avoiding hidden setting assumptions. Independent adversarial second pass passed.
